screens.title: Managing NTP with Chrony and Ansible
screens.narratorSegment: Accurate system time is surprisingly central to many services: logs, authentication, database consistency, and scheduled tasks all depend on clocks that agree. In Red Hat Enterprise Linux the chrony suite is the modern, resilient NTP implementation that handles intermittent networks and faster synchronization. In this lesson you'll learn how to ensure chrony is installed, configured, and kept consistent across servers using Ansible automation. We'll show the safe, idempotent approach of deploying an /etc/chrony. conf rendered from a Jinja2 template, using multiple NTP servers for redundancy, and using notify handlers to restart chronyd after configuration changes. You will also see common pitfalls such as firewall rules blocking UDP 123, forgetting to restart the service, and how makestep and driftfile behave when clocks are far off. By the end you'll be able to write a playbook that installs chrony, deploys a template with server entries, restarts the daemon when needed, and verifies synchronization using chronyc commands. Think about one server in your fleet that recently showed bad timestamps; this lesson helps you ensure that mistake doesn't happen again.

screens.title: Why Accurate System Time Matters
screens.narratorSegment: Accurate system time is a foundational piece of reliable systems. Logs from different hosts are meaningful only when timestamps align; without synchronized clocks it's difficult to correlate events across services. Security mechanisms such as Kerberos and TLS certificates depend on correct time to validate tickets and certificate lifetimes; a significant clock skew can cause authentication failures or rejected certificates. Databases and distributed systems use timestamps for ordering and consistency; diverging clocks can lead to data anomalies. Finally, many scheduled tasks and maintenance windows assume a shared clock; drift can cause jobs to run at unexpected moments. A concrete example is a multi-tier web application where access logs from the web server and the database must be correlated during incident response. If one host is minutes fast, tracing a user request across services becomes error-prone. A common misconception is that small drift is harmless; in reality, even seconds can break time-sensitive authentication or make audit trails unreliable. Key practice: treat time as part of your infrastructure, manage it through automation, and verify synchronization after changes so applications continue to behave predictably.

Module 6 › Chapter 6.6 › Why Accurate System Time Matters
Definition & impact

Accurate system time ensures events are ordered correctly, authentication tokens validate, and logs across hosts can be correlated reliably. Treat time drift as a potential cause of outages and security issues.

Concrete example

Correlating a failed login across a web tier and an authentication server requires aligned timestamps. A skewed host hides causality and complicates incident response.

Common misconception

Small drift is harmless. In fact, seconds of skew can break ticket-based authentication and certificate validation.

Key Takeaway

Make time synchronization part of your baseline automation to avoid hidden failures.

Practical checks
  • Confirm system clock with timedatectl or chronyc tracking after changes.
  • Ensure consistent time across logging, auth servers, and database nodes.
  • Automate deployment so all hosts share the same trusted NTP sources.
Try this

Identify one host in your environment, run chronyc tracking, and compare the reported offset with a known reference to see drift in practice.

screens.title: Why Chrony Replaces ntpd on RHEL
screens.narratorSegment: Chrony has become the preferred time synchronization suite on Red Hat platforms because it addresses real operational conditions. Unlike older daemons, chrony performs reliably on hosts with intermittent network connectivity, converges faster after startup, and adapts well when a system resumes from sleep or a sporadic connection. For example, a laptop or a container that only occasionally has network access will synchronize more quickly with chrony than with older implementations. Chrony also supports features such as kernel PPS synchronization for precise hardware timing and records clock drift in a driftfile so long-term correction is more accurate. A misconception to avoid is assuming all NTP clients behave identically; differences in algorithms and default directives matter for large fleets. In practice, choosing chrony on RHEL simplifies automation: your Ansible playbooks target a consistent package name and service name, and you can rely on faster convergence for routine deployments. Remember that configuration directives like makestep, driftfile, rtcsync, and server entries remain crucial for tuning behavior in your environment. Why Chrony Replaces ntpd on RHEL means chrony converges faster and handles intermittent networks better, offering operational advantages on rhel.. In practical terms, chrony's advantages for intermittent networks and faster sync. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Code example
- name: Ensure chrony package is installed
  ansible.builtin.package:
    name: chrony
    state: present

- name: Ensure chronyd service is running and enabled

screens.title: Manage /etc/chrony.conf with ansible.builtin.template
screens.narratorSegment: Managing the entire chrony configuration file via a rendered template is the most robust approach. While line-based edits can work, templates make the file's content explicit and reproducible. Using ansible. builtin. template you supply a Jinja2 source that iterates server entries and sets directives like driftfile, rtcsync, and makestep. This pattern makes it easy to inject inventory variables such as ntp_servers and to guarantee the file exactly matches your intended configuration. A concrete example is a template file that loops through ntp_servers and writes a server line with iburst for each. A common mistake is mixing lineinfile with a templated file elsewhere; prefer a single source of truth. Also remember to set file ownership and permissions appropriately. When the template changes, have the task notify a handler that restarts chronyd so changes take effect without unnecessary restarts. The template approach scales well when you manage many hosts with variable server lists or organization-specific pools. Manage /etc/chrony.conf with ansible.builtin.template means templates provide a single source of truth for chrony configuration and support dynamic variables for different host groups.. In practical terms, use jinja2 templates for robust, idempotent configuration management. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.6 › Templating chrony.conf
Jinja2 template example
# /etc/chrony.conf.j2
# Cohortia internal NTP servers
{% raw %}{% for server in ntp_servers %}{% endraw %}
server {{ server }} iburst
{% raw %}{% endfor %}{% endraw %}

driftfile /var/lib/chrony/drift
rtcsync
makestep 1 3
logdir /var/log/chrony
Use this template with ansible.builtin.template and supply ntp_servers as a variable in your playbook or inventory.
Why template over line edits
  • Ensures entire file matches desired state instead of piecemeal edits.
  • Makes it easy to include or exclude sections based on variables.
  • Simplifies auditability and rollbacks when stored in version control.
Key Takeaway

Render /etc/chrony.conf from a Jinja2 template for predictable, repeatable configuration across hosts.

screens.title: Key chrony.conf Directives
screens.narratorSegment: Understanding the main chrony. conf directives helps you tune synchronization behavior. The server or pool directives declare the NTP sources chronyd will use; using multiple entries provides redundancy and better accuracy. The driftfile records how the system clock typically gains or loses time and helps chrony compensate over time. Enabling rtcsync tells chrony to update the hardware real-time clock from the system clock, keeping the hardware clock consistent across reboots. The makestep directive instructs chrony to step, or make a larger adjustment, under controlled conditions — helpful for bringing a host with large initial drift back into sync in the first few updates. A common operational note is to include iburst on server lines to speed initial synchronization. Misconfiguring these directives or relying on a single unreachable server can prevent synchronization. By templating these directives and deploying them uniformly, you ensure consistent behavior across your fleet and avoid per-host surprises during incident response. keyIdea.text: server/pool set sources; driftfile records clock drift; rtcsync uses the hardware clock; makestep controls large adjustments.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.6 › chrony.conf Directives
Directive cards
server / pool
List NTP sources. Use multiple servers for redundancy and add iburst for fast startup.
driftfile
Records clock drift so chrony can apply long-term corrections.
rtcsync
Synchronize the hardware real-time clock from the system clock.
makestep
Allow controlled large clock steps during initial updates to correct large offsets.
Concrete example
server ntp1.internal.local iburst
server ntp2.internal.local iburst
driftfile /var/lib/chrony/drift
rtcsync
makestep 1 3
Key Takeaway

Pick multiple reliable servers and include directives that match your update policy and tolerance for large steps.

screens.title: Handlers and notify: Restart chronyd only when needed
screens.narratorSegment: A reliable playbook pattern is to deploy configuration files with ansible. builtin. template and notify a handler to restart the service only when the file changed. This avoids unnecessary restarts and reduces disruption to running processes. The template task should include notify: Restart chronyd, and a handlers section defines that action using ansible. builtin. service with state: restarted. A common error is forgetting to add the notify line, which means the new chrony server entries will not be loaded until a manual restart. Another nuance is to prefer restarted over reloaded when chronyd needs to fully reload the configuration, depending on your system's behavior. The handler runs at the end of the play so multiple changes trigger a single restart. For example, if you deploy package, template, and other tasks in one play, the handler ensures chronyd restarts once after all changes are complete, keeping the process efficient and predictable. Module 6 › Chapter 6.6 › Handlers & notify
Playbook snippet
tasks:
  - name: Deploy chrony configuration file
    ansible.builtin.template:
      src: chrony.conf.j2
      dest: /etc/chrony.conf
      owner: root
      group: root

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.6 › Hands-on Playbook
Playbook template
---
- name: Configure chrony for time synchronization
  hosts: app_servers
  become: true

  vars:
    ntp_servers:
      - ntp1.internal.local
      - ntp2.internal.local
      - 0.rhel.pool.ntp.org

  tasks:
    - name: Ensure chrony package is installed
      ansible.builtin.package:
        name: chrony
        state: present

    - name: Deploy chrony configuration file
      ansible.builtin.template:
        src: chrony.conf.j2
        dest: /etc/chrony.conf
        owner: root
        group: root
        mode: '0644'
      notify: Restart chronyd

    - name: Ensure chronyd service is running and enabled
      ansible.builtin.service:
        name: chronyd
        state: started
        enabled: yes

  handlers:
    - name: Restart chronyd
      ansible.builtin.service:
        name: chronyd
        state: restarted
Checklist before run
  • Define ntp_servers in play or inventory so the template renders server lines.
  • Ensure play targets the correct host group, e.g., app_servers or all.
  • Have a handler to restart chronyd so new configuration is applied.

screens.title: Common Mistakes and Safety Notes
screens.narratorSegment: The chapter lists several pitfalls that commonly disrupt time synchronization. First, configuring unreachable or unreliable NTP servers prevents chrony from syncing; always use a pool of trusted servers or internal servers you control. Second, firewall rules can silently block NTP traffic because NTP uses UDP port 123; if the daemon is running but sources are unreachable, inspect firewall settings and allow outbound UDP 123. Third, forgetting to notify a handler after changing chrony. conf means chronyd will continue using the old configuration until a manual restart; include the notify line in template tasks to avoid this. Fourth, very large time deviations may not be stepped automatically to avoid application issues; the makestep directive reduces this friction for initial corrections, but very large jumps sometimes require manual intervention such as a controlled chronyc -s or a maintenance window. Finally, if running chrony as a server, restrict clients with allow directives to prevent misuse. Each of these points maps directly to checks you should include in runbooks when automating time configuration. screens.title: Network and Security Considerations
screens.narratorSegment: When chrony is used as a client, ensure network paths to your NTP servers are open. NTP uses UDP port 123, so firewalls must permit outbound traffic on UDP 123 to the configured servers. If a host also provides NTP service, inbound UDP 123 must be allowed for legitimate clients. From a security perspective, if you run chrony as an NTP server, restrict which clients may query it using allow directives in chrony. conf to avoid abuse. Another operational point is to prefer internal NTP servers under your control when possible; relying solely on public pools may be acceptable as fallbacks but can introduce external dependencies. A common misconception is that opening UDP 123 broadly is safe; instead, apply least privilege and allow only known client networks to limit exposure. Include network and access checks in your automation: verify port connectivity and ensure allow directives are present where servers are exposed to other hosts. fullNarratorScript:
Accurate system time is surprisingly central to many services: logs, authentication, database consistency, and scheduled tasks all depend on clocks that agree. In Red Hat Enterprise Linux the chrony suite is the modern, resilient NTP implementation that handles intermittent networks and faster synchronization. In this lesson you'll learn how to ensure chrony is installed, configured, and kept consistent across servers using Ansible automation. We'll show the safe, idempotent approach of deploying an /etc/chrony. conf rendered from a Jinja2 template, using multiple NTP servers for redundancy, and using notify handlers to restart chronyd after configuration changes. You will also see common pitfalls such as firewall rules blocking UDP 123, forgetting to restart the service, and how makestep and driftfile behave when clocks are far off. By the end you'll be able to write a playbook that installs chrony, deploys a template with server entries, restarts the daemon when needed, and verifies synchronization using chronyc commands. Think about one server in your fleet that recently showed bad timestamps; this lesson helps you ensure that mistake doesn't happen again.

Accurate system time is a foundational piece of reliable systems. Logs from different hosts are meaningful only when timestamps align; without synchronized clocks it's difficult to correlate events across services. Security mechanisms such as Kerberos and TLS certificates depend on correct time to validate tickets and certificate lifetimes; a significant clock skew can cause authentication failures or rejected certificates. Databases and distributed systems use timestamps for ordering and consistency; diverging clocks can lead to data anomalies. Finally, many scheduled tasks and maintenance windows assume a shared clock; drift can cause jobs to run at unexpected moments. A concrete example is a multi-tier web application where access logs from the web server and the database must be correlated during incident response. If one host is minutes fast, tracing a user request across services becomes error-prone. A common misconception is that small drift is harmless; in reality, even seconds can break time-sensitive authentication or make audit trails unreliable. Key practice: treat time as part of your infrastructure, manage it through automation, and verify synchronization after changes so applications continue to behave predictably.

Chrony has become the preferred time synchronization suite on Red Hat platforms because it addresses real operational conditions. Unlike older daemons, chrony performs reliably on hosts with intermittent network connectivity, converges faster after startup, and adapts well when a system resumes from sleep or a sporadic connection. For example, a laptop or a container that only occasionally has network access will synchronize more quickly with chrony than with older implementations. Chrony also supports features such as kernel PPS synchronization for precise hardware timing and records clock drift in a driftfile so long-term correction is more accurate. A misconception to avoid is assuming all NTP clients behave identically; differences in algorithms and default directives matter for large fleets. In practice, choosing chrony on RHEL simplifies automation: your Ansible playbooks target a consistent package name and service name, and you can rely on faster convergence for routine deployments. Remember that configuration directives like makestep, driftfile, rtcsync, and server entries remain crucial for tuning behavior in your environment. Understanding the main chrony. conf directives helps you tune synchronization behavior. The server or pool directives declare the NTP sources chronyd will use; using multiple entries provides redundancy and better accuracy. The driftfile records how the system clock typically gains or loses time and helps chrony compensate over time. Enabling rtcsync tells chrony to update the hardware real-time clock from the system clock, keeping the hardware clock consistent across reboots. The chapter lists several pitfalls that commonly disrupt time synchronization. First, configuring unreachable or unreliable NTP servers prevents chrony from syncing; always use a pool of trusted servers or internal servers you control. Second, firewall rules can silently block NTP traffic because NTP uses UDP port 123; if the daemon is running but sources are unreachable, inspect firewall settings and allow outbound UDP 123. Third, forgetting to notify a handler after changing chrony. conf means chronyd will continue using the old configuration until a manual restart; include the notify line in template tasks to avoid this. Fourth, very large time deviations may not be stepped automatically to avoid application issues; the makestep directive reduces this friction for initial corrections, but very large jumps sometimes require manual intervention such as a controlled chronyc -s or a maintenance window. Finally, if running chrony as a server, restrict clients with allow directives to prevent misuse. Each of these points maps directly to checks you should include in runbooks when automating time configuration.
